# How Migratory Birds Navigate Precisely: Compasses, Maps, Cues, and Disturbances

Migratory birds achieve remarkably accurate travel by combining two different abilities. A compass supplies a heading—such as south-west—while a map-like system estimates where the bird is relative to its route or destination. The best-established compasses use the geomagnetic field, the Sun, stars, and polarized skylight. Position-fixing can draw on geomagnetic gradients, odors, landmarks, wind fields, and learned route information, but no single universal avian “GPS” has been demonstrated.

Precision is therefore produced by repeated comparison and correction rather than by one infallible cue. Adults with migration experience can correct large displacements, whereas juveniles often depend more heavily on inherited direction-and-duration programs or route beacons. Natural disturbances—including crosswinds, storms, cloud, fog, magnetic storms, and local magnetic anomalies—change cue availability or push birds off course. Artificial light and radio-frequency electromagnetic noise have the clearest evidence for directly disturbing orientation; conventional noise, air pollution, habitat loss, and landmark change more often show indirect effects on stopover use, energy budgets, connectivity, or migration timing.

This report first separates directional orientation from geographic positioning. It then examines magnetic, celestial, olfactory, visual, wind, and possible acoustic cues; explains how birds calibrate and substitute among them; compares the evidence across species and age classes; and finally distinguishes demonstrated human impacts from plausible but still untested mechanisms.

## Direction and location are different navigation problems

### A compass gives a direction; a map gives a position

A compass answers: “Which direction should I maintain?” A map or position-fixing system answers: “Where am I, and how is my present position related to the goal?” This distinction is central because a bird can fly in a consistent inherited direction without knowing its exact geographic location. Conversely, a bird that detects displacement must have some way to obtain positional information before it can choose a corrective heading.

Reviews of avian navigation describe these as sequential but interacting operations. The map step estimates present position and its relation to the destination; the compass step identifies the direction to follow. On a first migration, however, the map step may be replaced or supplemented by an inherited program specifying a direction, a duration, and sometimes a programmed change in direction over the season ([European Physical Journal review of bird navigation](https://doi.org/10.1140/epjs/s11734-022-00610-w); [Journal of Ornithology review, 2025](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40462-025-00543-8)).

The distinction does not imply that birds carry a literal map with latitude and longitude. A “map” may be a learned association between magnetic values and geographic regions, a comparison of wind-borne odor mixtures, a sequence of landscape features, or a simpler rule such as “this field value is stronger than anything previously experienced, so I must be east or north of the familiar range.” Such a rule may be enough to return a bird to a familiar corridor without calculating an exact coordinate.

### Displacement experiments reveal position correction

The strongest evidence for map-like navigation comes from translocation experiments. Researchers move birds to unfamiliar places, remove or alter candidate cues, and test whether the birds continue their normal direction or compensate toward the breeding or wintering area.

Eurasian reed warblers provide one of the clearest examples. In a double-blind experiment, 57 spring migrants were moved about 1,000 km east from Rybachy in the eastern Baltic to Zvenigorod near Moscow. Untreated and sham-operated birds changed their headings toward the breeding range. Birds whose ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve—V1—had been cut did not make the correction; they retained the capture-site direction. The result shows that V1-transmitted information is required for this large-scale position correction, but it does not identify whether the information is magnetic, olfactory, or another sensory signal ([Kishkinev et al., 2013](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0065847)).

The same experiment also separated this map-related pathway from the basic magnetic compass. In European robins and bobolinks, disrupting V1 did not abolish magnetic-compass orientation. Conversely, inactivating the forebrain region called Cluster N prevented magnetic-compass use while leaving sun and star compasses functional. V1 is therefore not simply the nerve carrying the ordinary magnetic heading signal.

A continental-scale example comes from Gambel’s white-crowned sparrows. Thirty birds—15 adults and 15 juveniles—were displaced about 3,700 km from the western to the eastern United States and tracked by radio. Adults corrected toward their expected wintering grounds, whereas juveniles continued in their inherited southerly direction. The study demonstrates a learned map extending at least across a continent, but it did not identify the sensory cue supplying that map. Magnetic intensity, celestial information, and olfaction all remained possible explanations ([Thorup et al., 2007](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2084305/)).

Other juvenile studies show that the boundary between inherited orientation and true position correction is not absolute. Juvenile blackcaps, garden warblers, and willow warblers displaced about 1,100 km from Denmark to the Faroe Islands changed their headings in ways consistent with compensation. Yet the scatter was too large to determine whether they were heading toward the capture site, the wintering grounds, or an intermediate route. The authors therefore left open three possibilities: a primitive form of true navigation, route signposts, or a less specific displacement response ([Thorup et al., 2011](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0017903)).

Satellite tracking of common cuckoos produced another nuanced result. Young and adult cuckoos were displaced about 1,800 km east. Young displaced birds ended up significantly west of control birds, consistent with partial compensation, and young and adults traveled in broadly similar directions toward the normal route. Individual tracks ranged from little correction to substantial correction, and the sensory cue remained unknown ([Willemoes et al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-64230-x)).

These studies establish position correction, not a universal mechanism. A bird may compensate for a displacement without knowing its exact distance or coordinate. In the reed-warbler magnetic experiments, for example, the researchers explicitly discuss a rule-of-thumb interpretation: an unfamiliar combination of field values may simply signal that the bird has moved beyond a familiar boundary and should return in a particular direction ([Kishkinev et al., 2021](https://www.courthousenews.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/Bird-migration-geomagnetic-cues-Current-Biology.pdf)).

### Precision is a behavioral outcome, not one fixed number

“Precise navigation” can mean several different measurable outcomes:

| Navigation task | What researchers measure | What it establishes |
|---|---|---|
| Directional orientation | Mean heading, angular concentration, or vanishing bearing | Whether birds choose a non-random direction |
| Position correction | Change in heading after displacement | Whether birds detect that they are geographically misplaced |
| Route maintenance | Deviation from a preferred corridor | How well birds resist wind and environmental disturbance |
| Corridor recovery | Turning back toward a familiar route | Whether learned position information helps restore a route |
| Terminal localization | Arrival at a colony, breeding site, or stopover | Whether local landmarks or learned cues pinpoint a destination |

A narrow track does not automatically prove a map. Nine bar-tailed godwits tracked from Alaska across the Pacific had strongly concentrated initial headings around 193° and followed a corridor less than 1,800 km wide—only about 10–15% of the Pacific’s width between the tropics. They completed oceanic flights of thousands of kilometers, but the study could not determine whether their accuracy came from a magnetic map, celestial heading, inherited route program, wind compensation, or a combination ([Gill et al., 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2664343/)).

Likewise, a correction response does not prove that birds calculate a two-dimensional coordinate. It shows that the available cues changed in a way the bird associated with a geographic displacement. The exact spatial resolution, distance estimate, and computational rule remain species-dependent and are not available as a single cross-species accuracy bound.

## Compass cues for maintaining direction

### The geomagnetic inclination compass

The avian magnetic compass differs from a human compass. It does not primarily detect magnetic north and south as opposite poles. Instead, it responds to the axis and inclination—the angle at which field lines enter or leave the Earth—so that birds can distinguish poleward from equatorward directions. This is why it is called an inclination compass ([Frontiers review of avian magnetoreception](https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2021.667000); [Wiltschko et al., 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4305412/)).

The compass is light-dependent. Behavioral experiments summarized in recent reviews show orientation under ultraviolet, violet, blue, turquoise, and green light, roughly through 565 nanometers, but disorientation under red light. This dependence is consistent with a retinal photochemical mechanism involving light-sensitive cryptochrome molecules and radical pairs. The radical-pair hypothesis is the leading explanation: light excites a retinal molecule, electron spins form a radical pair, and the geomagnetic field changes the pair’s reaction probabilities in a direction-dependent way.

The molecular mechanism is not settled. Cry4a from the European robin has shown magnetic sensitivity in vitro, and its expression changes during the migratory season, but in-vitro sensitivity does not prove that Cry4a is the functional receptor in a living migrating bird. The route from a retinal chemical reaction to a neural directional signal also remains incompletely understood ([PNAS review of the avian magnetic compass](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10334787/)).

European robins are the classic example. Earlier experiments established that robins orient with a light-dependent magnetic compass during migration. More recent work shows that the system is plastic. Robins acclimated to a local field of about 47 microteslas could still orient after exposure to much weaker or stronger fields, including 4 and 150 microteslas. Yet they failed to orient in an intermediate field they had not experienced before. This indicates that the usable intensity range is flexible but calibrated by experience rather than being an unlimited global scale ([Frontiers review of avian magnetoreception](https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2021.667000)).

The European robin also illustrates calibration across life stages. Forty-one hand-raised robins that had failed to develop a functional compass during their first autumn migration were divided between natural-cue and indoor-control conditions. The 22 birds later exposed to the natural sky oriented in their expected spring direction at 56°, whereas the 19 birds kept indoors remained random. The study supports delayed recalibration of the magnetic compass by celestial information, although the exact external reference could not be isolated ([Alert et al., 2015](https://www.nature.com/articles/srep14323)).

Magnetic field intensity and inclination can therefore serve two different roles. The light-dependent system is strongly supported as a directional compass. A different magnetic sensory pathway, often associated with the trigeminal system or putative iron-containing receptors, has been proposed for position information. The existence and function of that second receptor remain contested.

### The Sun compass

A sun compass uses the Sun’s azimuth—the horizontal direction of the Sun—but the Sun moves across the sky during the day. Birds solve this by combining solar position with an internal circadian clock. The same solar azimuth means different compass directions at different times, so the clock allows the bird to compensate for the Sun’s apparent movement. Young birds learn the relationship between the Sun’s path and time of day, and this calibration changes with season and latitude ([Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution review](https://doi.org/10.3389/fevo.2020.00078)).

The sun compass is most useful in daylight and twilight, although its calibration can occur at sunrise or sunset. Clouds, fog, dense haze, and urban skyglow can obscure or distort the solar reference. Birds may still use the geomagnetic compass when the Sun is unavailable, but the balance between cues depends on species, experience, and the visibility of the horizon.

The Sun also produces a pattern of polarized skylight. The strongest polarization occurs in a band roughly 90° from the Sun, and this pattern can remain visible when the Sun itself is hidden but the sky is not completely obscured. Polarized light is therefore especially important around sunrise and sunset, when it can provide a stable directional reference for calibrating the magnetic and celestial compasses.

### Polarized skylight as a calibration cue

Polarized light is not usually a separate long-distance route compass in the same sense as the magnetic or stellar compass. Its clearest demonstrated role is calibration. A bird can compare the polarization pattern near the horizon with its magnetic heading, creating a common geographic reference for several compasses.

A review of cue-conflict experiments concluded that young and premigratory birds often give celestial cues high salience and use them to recalibrate the magnetic compass. During migration, many experiments instead found the magnetic field acting as the primary reference for calibrating celestial compasses. The apparent contradiction largely tracks the bird’s access to the sunset horizon: birds that saw the whole sunset sky tended to recalibrate their magnetic compass, whereas birds tested in funnels or cages with the critical horizon region blocked often used the magnetic field to recalibrate celestial cues ([Muheim et al., 2006](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16354773/)).

This proposed hierarchy is not universal. In a field experiment at Falsterbo, juvenile garden warblers were exposed around sunset to a magnetic field shifted by 90°. They had a clear horizon, yet neither their initial radio-tracked orientations nor their vanishing bearings differed from controls. The experimenters could not exclude the possibility that the birds relied on a previously calibrated star compass rather than recalibrating during the treatment. The result demonstrates that cue-conflict outcomes depend on species, season, prior learning, sky access, and experimental context ([Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience](https://doi.org/10.3389/fnbeh.2016.00029)).

### The star compass

Nocturnal migrants can learn a star compass from the apparent rotation of the night sky. The crucial information is not a particular constellation but the center around which the stars rotate. In the Northern Hemisphere, that center is close to geographic north. After learning the rotation, birds can use the learned stellar pattern even when they cannot see the rotation occurring during an actual migration night.

Indigo buntings provide the best-known example. In planetarium experiments, hand-raised buntings learned a false celestial rotation center and subsequently oriented relative to that artificial “north.” Even after six months in an outdoor aviary with an unobstructed natural sky, they did not switch to the real celestial rotation center. This suggests a sensitive learning period and a relatively fixed star compass once established ([Alert et al., 2015](https://www.nature.com/articles/srep14323); [Tyagi and Bhardwaj review](https://journals.ansfoundation.org/index.php/jans/article/download/2684/2030/6901)).

The indigo-bunting result contrasts with the European robin experiment. Robins that had not established a functional compass could later acquire one after natural celestial exposure, whereas buntings that had already learned an incorrect star compass did not readily replace it. The difference may reflect species-specific plasticity, but a more likely explanation is the state of the compass: an unformed system can be calibrated more readily than an already established but incorrect stellar reference.

A star compass is independent of the time of day once learned, unlike the sun compass. It is nevertheless vulnerable to clouds, fog, moonlight, skyglow, and any change that obscures the rotation pattern or reduces the visibility of the stars. The importance of stars within approximately 35° of the rotation center has been reported in reviewed experiments, but only a small number of nocturnal songbird species have been studied directly.

### Wind is a movement cue, not usually a compass

Wind does not tell a bird where geographic north is, but it changes the relationship between the bird’s heading and its ground track. A bird flying north-east through a westward crosswind may need to point north-west to maintain a north-east ground course. Wind can therefore be both a resource and a disturbance.

Migrants often choose departure times with favorable winds. Nine bar-tailed godwits leaving Alaska for the Pacific timed departures to weather systems producing tailwinds. Wind directions at the departure region were concentrated around 174°, and bird departure directions were strongly correlated with them. This is evidence that birds use atmospheric conditions to choose when and perhaps how to begin a crossing, not evidence that wind alone supplies geographic position ([Gill et al., 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2664343/)).

Wind can also support a route while increasing the danger of displacement. A tailwind improves groundspeed, while a crosswind changes the lateral position of the track. Birds can respond by changing heading, airspeed, altitude, departure timing, or stopover decisions. These corrections are often easiest to observe in free flight, where birds integrate wind with whatever map or route information they possess.

## Map cues for determining geographic position

### Geomagnetic gradients: intensity, inclination, and declination

The Earth’s magnetic field changes across geography. Total intensity and inclination generally vary along a broad north–south axis, while declination—the difference between geographic north and magnetic north—often varies more strongly east–west. In theory, a bird could combine two gradients to estimate position, much as two coordinates identify a point on a map.

The difficulty is that the gradients do not form a regular global grid. Their geometry varies by region, and different field parameters can change in similar directions or produce repeated values at distant locations. Magnetic anomalies caused by local crustal rocks can disrupt the broad dipole pattern. They may serve as landmarks for some animals, but their navigational effect depends on anomaly size, intensity, spatial scale, and species ([Journal of Comparative Physiology review](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00359-021-01529-8)).

Eurasian reed warblers provide unusually direct evidence for a geomagnetic position cue. In a virtual-displacement experiment, experienced birds were exposed to a magnetic field simulating a location about 2,700 km north-east of the capture site. The researchers changed inclination, declination, and total intensity together so that the combination matched a real place. Birds shifted their mean orientation from about 133° in the natural field to about 228° in the simulated field, a significant change consistent with reorientation toward their normal migratory corridor.

A declination-only treatment did not produce a significant shift: birds oriented at about 113° in the natural field and 142° after a 10° declination change, with overlapping confidence intervals. The result suggests that birds may reject a magnetic combination that does not occur naturally, or may give greater weight to intensity and inclination than to declination alone. Earlier reed-warbler experiments found a response to declination, while other species did not. The most defensible conclusion is that declination can contribute to position information in some contexts, but it is not a universal longitude coordinate ([Kishkinev et al., 2021](https://www.courthousenews.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/Bird-migration-geomagnetic-cues-Current-Biology.pdf)).

The reed-warbler experiment also exposes a conceptual limit. The birds may have extrapolated learned gradients beyond their previous experience, as the authors argue, but a simpler rule may explain the same behavior: values outside the familiar range signal that the bird is displaced in a particular direction. Both mechanisms would produce adaptive correction without requiring precise coordinate calculation.

The evidence is strongest for intermediate-scale magnetic position information. A review suggests that magnetic resolution may be sufficient over tens of kilometers or more, but too coarse for small-scale navigation near a destination. At the terminal scale, birds are more likely to rely on landmarks, odors, spatial memory, or local habitat structure ([Frontiers review of avian navigation](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/ecology-and-evolution/articles/10.3389/fevo.2021.740027/full)).

### Olfaction and wind-borne odor information

Birds have a well-established sense of smell, but the way odor supports navigation differs among taxa. The strongest classic evidence comes from homing pigeons, not migratory birds. Pigeons raised at a loft can associate recurring wind directions with mixtures of airborne chemicals. After displacement, the odor mixture at the release site may indicate how the bird is displaced relative to home.

This does not necessarily require every site to have a unique chemical “fingerprint.” Atmospheric chemistry is too dynamic for a simple mosaic of permanent local signatures. A more plausible model uses several overlapping gradients: marine compounds, vegetation-derived terpenes, and anthropogenic aromatic compounds. Their ratios and directions of change can supply a regional vector.

Measurements around a pigeon loft near Pisa illustrate the physical basis. Dimethyl sulfide (DMS), largely associated with marine emissions, had an estimated atmospheric 1/e transport distance of about 88 km under the reported conditions. Xylenes had an estimated distance of about 33 km, while the more reactive compounds limonene and isoprene decayed over about 2 km and 11 km, respectively. DMS and some aromatic compounds could therefore form regional gradients across roughly 50–100 km. The study also measured different horizontal and vertical mixtures at the ground and at about 180 m altitude ([Zannoni et al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-72525-2)).

The same study released 174 inexperienced pigeons 50–70 km from their loft and recovered 143 usable GPS tracks. In 135 tracks, the first 10 km of flight showed a small but statistically significant association between initial deviation from west and the modeled ratio of time air masses had spent over sea versus land. The authors interpreted this as consistent with a DMS gradient, but air chemistry was not measured during the releases. It is therefore evidence for a plausible environmental mechanism, not a direct identification of the chemical cue.

Migratory gulls provide stronger evidence that olfaction can support large-scale position correction. Adult lesser black-backed gulls were moved about 1,080 km west of their normal migratory corridor. Gulls with intact olfactory nerves and gulls with the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve sectioned oriented toward the population-specific corridor. Gulls with olfactory nerves sectioned retained a southerly migratory preference but failed to correct the longitudinal displacement. Olfaction was therefore needed for correction in this unfamiliar setting, while it was not needed for the basic directional program ([Wikelski et al., 2015](https://www.nature.com/articles/srep17061)).

A second study tracked 20 lesser black-backed gulls displaced 850–1,000 km and used FLEXPART atmospheric particle modeling to estimate whether birds encountered air transported from their familiar migratory corridor. Among 17 birds migrating south from Helgoland, eight of 11 birds with intact olfaction that received modeled corridor particles reoriented, compared with one of six anosmic birds. The association was non-random, and detailed tracks showed turns toward the modeled plume. This supports wind-borne odor information, but cannot distinguish a learned olfactory map from plume following ([Frontiers olfactory-navigation study](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/behavioral-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnbeh.2016.00175/full)).

A true olfactory map and plume following make different predictions. A map compares local odor conditions with learned wind–odor associations and can work even when the wind does not carry a continuous plume from the destination. Plume following is simpler: the bird detects an odor concentration and flies upwind toward its source. It works only when winds transport odor from the destination to the bird. The available evidence supports olfactory information but does not establish which computational strategy dominates.

Olfactory dependence is also conditional. In the gull study, anosmic birds corrected a displacement within Russia as effectively as controls, probably because the release region was familiar or within the normal corridor. Adult Eurasian reed warblers moved 1,004 km east still corrected their initial direction after their olfactory nerves were chemically impaired. Their headings did not differ significantly from controls. These counterexamples show that birds can substitute among cues and that an olfactory map is not universal even within long-distance migrants ([Journal of Ornithology reed-warbler study](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10336-019-01698-z)).

The specific question of an olfactory map in migrating garden warblers requires caution. Garden warblers are central to experiments on inherited migratory direction and celestial–magnetic calibration, but the evidence supplied here does not provide a direct garden-warbler olfactory-nerve manipulation demonstrating a migratory map. Evidence from pigeons, gulls, shearwaters, and other seabirds cannot simply be transferred to garden warblers.

### Visual landmarks and topography

Visual information is most useful when the bird is near land or a familiar route. Coastlines, rivers, mountain ranges, islands, valleys, wetlands, and other conspicuous features can act as landmarks or signposts. Birds may also use optic flow—the movement of the visual scene across the retina—to estimate displacement and speed.

The evidence for long-distance landmark use is stronger in route-correction models than in direct cue-isolation experiments. Visual landmarks have been proposed as a mechanism for wind-drift compensation: lateral movement of landmarks across the visual field can reveal that a crosswind is pushing the bird away from its preferred corridor. This mechanism becomes difficult over featureless ocean, pack ice, high-altitude cloud, or at night.

Radar observations at the Strait of Messina illustrate the consequence of reduced visibility. During spring migration, 96% of tracks occurred in clear conditions and had a mean direction of 57.3°. The 4% of tracks in fog had a mean direction of 80.7°, and fog increased directional scatter. Birds also changed their wind response under fog, sometimes under-compensating and sometimes over-compensating for crosswind. The study cannot prove that landmarks caused the difference, but the pattern is consistent with reduced visual route information ([Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/ecology-and-evolution/articles/10.3389/fevo.2021.745002/full)).

Bar-tailed and Hudsonian godwits show why visual landmarks cannot be the whole explanation. Both undertake long oceanic flights with few or no stable topographic features. Their tracks demonstrate strong directional control and wind compensation, but the studies do not isolate celestial, magnetic, olfactory, wave, or atmospheric cues. Visual landmarks may help near departure or arrival, while other cues maintain the route offshore.

### Wind fields, pressure, temperature, and humidity

Atmospheric conditions can provide information about movement context even when they do not constitute a map. Wind direction and speed reveal the energetic cost of alternative headings. Temperature, humidity, pressure, and the boundaries between broad circulation systems may provide environmental signposts. Whether migrants use such variables as geographic coordinates remains unresolved.

The route of a bird can also be constrained by the energetic consequences of being displaced. A bird may not need to know its exact longitude if it recognizes that it has crossed a dangerous route boundary, entered an unfavorable wind regime, or is approaching a region where stopover habitat is scarce. Position and risk are then linked.

### Auditory cues and infrasound

Infrasound is sound below approximately 20 hertz. Marine microbaroms, often around 0.1–0.6 hertz, arise from interactions between opposing ocean waves and can propagate for thousands of kilometers. In theory, a bird could use their direction, intensity, or spatial gradient as a beacon or as information about distant storms, swell, or coastline geometry.

The mechanism remains speculative for migration. A review proposed three possible map roles—acoustic beacons, acoustic landmarks, and gradients—but emphasized that navigational use was untested. Low-frequency hearing has been measured in only a small number of bird species, and no empirical infrasonic sensitivity data were available for seabirds in that review ([Patrick et al., 2021](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/ecology-and-evolution/articles/10.3389/fevo.2021.740027/full)).

A 2023 study of 89 wandering albatrosses supplied an important but limited field result. GPS tracks and modeled microbarom soundscapes showed that albatrosses preferentially selected flight segments with higher modeled infrasound pressure, even after accounting for wind. The best-supported model included both wind and sound pressure, with a QIC weight of 0.99 compared with less than 0.001 for the wind-only model. The result suggests sensitivity to long-range infrasound, perhaps because louder microbaroms indicate distant wave and wind conditions favorable for soaring ([Gillies et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2218679120)).

This is not a direct demonstration of an infrasound compass. The birds were foraging rather than migrating, albatross hearing at microbarom frequencies had not been measured, and the birds may have responded to correlated variables such as barometric pressure or distant weather. No primary migration study in the evidence considered here demonstrates that anthropogenic infrasound changes migratory direction.

## Cue integration, calibration, and error correction

### Birds do not use a fixed universal cue hierarchy

A single hierarchy would be attractive: perhaps birds always trust magnetic information first, then stars, then landmarks. Experiments do not support such a universal rule. Cue weighting changes with species, age, season, prior learning, horizon visibility, weather, route, and whether the bird is traveling through familiar or unfamiliar space.

The apparent conflict between magnetic and celestial calibration studies illustrates this. Some experiments show celestial cues recalibrating the magnetic compass; others show the magnetic field recalibrating celestial compasses. A review found that the difference often depended on whether birds could see the polarized-light band near the sunset horizon. Full horizon access favored celestial calibration of the magnetic compass, while restricted access favored magnetic calibration of other compasses ([Muheim et al., 2006](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16354773/)).

The Falsterbo garden-warbler experiment complicates even that interpretation. Full horizon access and a 90° magnetic shift did not produce detectable recalibration. The birds may have relied on a previously learned star compass, or the timing and geometry of the conflict may not have supplied the relevant calibration conditions. The result is evidence against a simple rule, not evidence that calibration is unimportant.

### Calibration links independent compass systems

Birds benefit when their separate compasses agree. A juvenile may learn the rotation of the stars, observe the Sun’s path, and experience the local magnetic field during the same developmental period. The three systems can then be cross-referenced.

The European robin experiment demonstrates this plasticity in a bird whose initial compass had not formed. Exposure to the natural sky during late winter and spring allowed the birds to orient by the magnetic field in the appropriate spring direction. The authors interpret the natural celestial cues as calibrating the magnetic compass, although their design did not isolate stars, Sun, polarization, or other celestial information.

Indigo buntings demonstrate the cost of calibration errors. Once the star compass had been established around an artificial rotation center, later exposure to the natural sky did not restore correct orientation. An incorrect reference can therefore become stable rather than being continuously overwritten.

Calibration may also occur repeatedly. Migrating songbirds have been reported to recalibrate their magnetic compass from twilight cues, and the proposed role of polarized light provides a mechanism for daily alignment. Yet not all species show the same response, and some experiments have failed to reproduce a common calibration hierarchy.

### Inherited programs become learned maps and beacons

The direction of migration is often partly inherited. Hand-reared German garden warblers followed the same sequence of seasonal compass directions as free-living birds, even without learning a route from adults. This demonstrates an endogenous program but not a complete position-fixing map ([Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution](https://doi.org/10.3389/fevo.2020.00078)).

Experience adds flexibility. Adult white-crowned sparrows corrected a 3,700-km displacement, while juveniles followed their inherited southerly direction. Adult gulls corrected unfamiliar longitudinal displacement using olfactory information, whereas birds in familiar regions could substitute other cues. These results suggest that the “map” is built gradually through repeated exposure to landscapes, odors, field values, winds, and destination regions.

The age pattern is not uniform. Juvenile blackcaps, garden warblers, and willow warblers showed some correction after an 1,100-km displacement, and young cuckoos partially corrected an 1,800-km displacement. A 2025 review therefore proposes that first-time migrants may use a sequence of beacons rather than a complete geographic map. A beacon might be a geomagnetic threshold, an odor corridor, a coastline, a weather regime, or a learned environmental transition. The available data do not yet reveal how accurately first-year birds locate themselves along such routes ([Frontiers in Physiology review, 2025](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2025.1562569/full)).

### Redundancy allows substitution

Redundancy is valuable because no cue works everywhere. Stars disappear in cloud; visual landmarks disappear over water; odors become intermittent; magnetic information can be altered by radio-frequency fields; winds can overwhelm a heading; artificial light can modify the celestial environment.

The gull experiments show substitution especially clearly. After an unfamiliar westward displacement, olfaction was necessary for corridor correction. After a displacement within a familiar region, anosmic birds corrected as well as controls. A bird can therefore use one cue when the situation is novel and another when the route is familiar.

Seabirds with impaired olfaction have also been reported to take longer to home and to follow coastlines more closely, suggesting that visual topography can partly replace olfactory information. In Eurasian reed warblers, however, anosmia did not prevent a correction response after a 1,004-km displacement. The direction of substitution is therefore not fixed across species.

Neural reviews propose that hippocampal systems may interact with map and compass representations, while the caudolateral nidopallium may help weigh conflicting information and respond to unexpected circumstances. These are useful hypotheses about integration, not established universal circuit mechanisms ([Mouritsen et al., 2016](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-physiol-021115-105054)).

### Wind-drift compensation is a continuous control problem

A flying bird’s ground track is the sum of its airspeed vector and the wind vector:

\[
\mathbf{v}_{\text{ground}}=\mathbf{v}_{\text{air}}+\mathbf{v}_{\text{wind}}.
\]

If the wind pushes the bird sideways, maintaining a desired ground track requires changing the air heading, airspeed, altitude, or route. The bird may deliberately accept drift when the energetic cost is low, then compensate more strongly when a route boundary, coastline, barrier, or destination becomes important.

Hudsonian godwits provide the strongest quantitative example over open ocean. Satellite tracking followed 25 adults from Chiloé Island, Chile, toward the northern Gulf of Mexico on flights longer than 7,000 km. Across 676 classified flight segments, full compensation was the most common behavior at 41.1%. Partial compensation accounted for 23.5%, overcompensation 16.0%, full drifting 9.4%, supported flight 8.1%, and overdrift 1.9%. Overall, the birds allowed approximately 39.4% of potential drift.

Compensation remained common over the Pacific, despite the scarcity of visual landmarks, and did not increase simply as the birds approached North America. Cumulative crosswinds did not predict the location where birds crossed the northern Gulf of Mexico. The authors infer that birds may respond to geographic risk: westward displacement over the Pacific could lead to energetic depletion or stranding, whereas divergence becomes less costly near land ([Linscott et al., 2022](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40462-022-00310-z)).

The godwits also selected altitude according to wind support. Their ground speeds were best explained by choosing the altitude with maximum support in the preferred direction while remaining at or below about 3,000 m. Most modeled locations were at 100 or 750 m, and the predicted airspeed was 12.70 m/s, with a 95% confidence interval of 12.14–13.27 m/s. The altitude estimates were inferred from ground speed and wind models, not directly measured.

The results show that apparent navigational precision can arise from a combination of position-dependent risk and continuous wind correction. They do not reveal whether the bird uses a geomagnetic map, celestial reference, odor, wave pattern, or several of these cues to know where the route boundaries lie.

### Which cues offer the greatest precision, range, and resilience?

No experiment has ranked all cues on a common scale. The comparison below therefore uses the strongest available proxy for each system rather than a universal accuracy score.

| Cue system | Best-supported function | Effective scale or condition | Main strength | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Magnetic inclination compass | Maintain heading | Day or night when suitable short-wavelength light is available | Works without landmarks and is broadly available | Light-dependent; receptor mechanism unresolved; RF and field disturbances can interfere |
| Sun and polarized skylight | Heading and calibration | Daylight, twilight, and visible horizon | Strong geographic reference and clock compensation | Clouds, fog, haze, and horizon obstruction reduce access |
| Star compass | Nocturnal heading | Clear night sky after developmental learning | Time-independent geographic-north reference | Learned during a sensitive period; obscured by cloud, skyglow, and moonlight |
| Geomagnetic gradients | Intermediate-scale position correction | Regions with informative intensity, inclination, or declination gradients | Potentially available over land and ocean, day and night | Gradients are irregular; evidence is species-specific and may reflect rules of thumb |
| Olfaction | Corridor recovery and regional position information | Familiar odor–wind environment; suitable atmospheric transport | Can provide information where visual landmarks are absent | Odors are turbulent, transformed, and species-dependent; map versus plume remains unresolved |
| Visual landmarks and topography | Route correction and terminal localization | Near coasts, rivers, mountains, islands, or familiar landscapes | Can provide fine local positional information | Limited over open ocean, at high altitude, at night, or in fog |
| Wind and atmospheric cues | Timing, route choice, speed, and drift correction | Whenever wind fields are measurable through flight effects | Immediate energetic information and altitude options | Wind is not by itself a demonstrated geographic map |
| Infrasound | Possible long-range environmental beacon | Particularly plausible over oceans | Theoretical range of hundreds to thousands of kilometers | Migration-navigation causality and species-specific hearing remain unestablished |

The most disturbance-resistant single directional cue is probably the magnetic compass in its normal operating conditions, because it does not require a clear sky or nearby landmarks. The most precise local cues are likely visual landmarks and learned odors, but their range is shorter. The widest theoretical range belongs to geomagnetic gradients and infrasound, although the latter has the weakest migration-specific evidence. In practice, the most resilient strategy is multimodal integration: a bird uses different cues at different spatial scales and substitutes when one becomes unreliable.

## Natural disturbances and environmental limits

### Geomagnetic storms and anomalies

Geomagnetic storms change the field over time and can add noise to a spatial signal. A bird using intensity or inclination as a map must distinguish geographic differences from temporal fluctuations. Reed-warbler authors noted daily and between-day intensity variation commonly around ±30–100 nanoteslas, implying that a small spatial gradient could be hidden by natural field noise.

Large-scale evidence links magnetic disturbance to vagrancy, especially in autumn. A hierarchical analysis of 2,226,936 banding records from 152 North American landbird species between 1960 and 2019 found that a two-standard-deviation increase in geomagnetic disturbance corresponded, for a typical species, to a 24% increase in the median predicted vagrancy index and a 250% increase in spatiotemporally rare records—from 2% to 5% of records. Positive species-specific estimates occurred for 83% of the 150 species included in the fall analysis ([Scientific Reports geomagnetic-disturbance study](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-26586-0)).

The seasonal effect was not symmetrical. For 124 spring-migration species, evidence for a relationship between vagrancy and geomagnetic disturbance was weak. Sampling sites may have missed the earliest part of spring migration, when magnetic orientation could be especially important. Magnetic disturbance is therefore a contributor, not a complete explanation of vagrancy.

Geomagnetic anomalies can have two opposite effects. A local anomaly may distort a bird’s position estimate, but it may also act as a learned landmark if birds encounter it repeatedly. Large anomalies can produce similar field signatures at separated locations, potentially causing a bird to interpret the wrong place as its destination. Neither outcome is expected for every species or spatial scale.

### Wind, storms, and atmospheric circulation

Unfavorable winds can increase energy expenditure, delay departure, create lateral displacement, and force a bird to land or change route. A review of first-time migrants emphasizes that protracted opposing winds and storms can be especially difficult for inexperienced birds relying on inherited direction-and-duration programs.

Radio-tracking at a German coastal stopover showed how weather affects several stages of migration. Among 275 songbirds—garden warblers, greater whitethroats, and sedge warblers—178 flights were analyzed. Birds departed more often under favorable wind and cloud conditions, selected offshore or coastal routes according to wind support, and were more likely to interrupt flight under overcast skies or headwinds. Fifteen garden warblers and nine greater whitethroats crossed offshore, while every tracked sedge warbler followed the coast. Different individuals sometimes selected different routes during the same night ([Proceedings of the Royal Society B](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9905979/)).

Weather can alter the meaning of the same sensory cue. A tailwind may permit a direct route, while a crosswind may require compensation. A storm may be a danger, a barrier, or a source of favorable wind depending on species and morphology. Soaring seabirds may seek wind and waves but avoid the strongest winds, which can cause stranding or structural injury ([Gillies et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2218679120)).

### Cloud, fog, and visibility

Cloud cover affects solar, polarized-light, and stellar cues. Fog also obscures landmarks and can change the bird’s ability to judge drift. The magnetic compass may remain available, but the bird loses redundancy and may have to rely more heavily on a cue that is less precise in a particular region.

The available large-scale telemetry evidence supports an interaction rather than a simple additive effect. A dataset of 93 individually tracked birds from five nocturnally migrating species found greater route deviation during nocturnal than diurnal flight, a positive association between wind speed and deviation, and greater deviation at lower magnetic inclination. Under heavy cloud, route deviation became substantially more sensitive to magnetic inclination, suggesting that birds were more dependent on the magnetic system when celestial cues were obscured. Species differed significantly: bar-tailed godwits had the lowest deviation and tundra swans the highest ([Ohio State University telemetry analysis](https://kb.osu.edu/items/cd7af9cb-94ec-4341-a964-8c5bd443e437)).

Fog at the Strait of Messina produced a similar interaction between visibility and wind correction. Birds showed a different mean direction and more variable lateral compensation under fog than under clear skies. The study could not measure altitude or the exact spatial distribution of the fog, so the mechanism remains inferential.

### Seasonal stage, experience, and route displacement

The same cue can have different value at different migration stages. A juvenile following an inherited program may not react to a displacement that an experienced adult corrects. A bird approaching an unfamiliar barrier may prioritize route safety over energetic efficiency. A bird near a familiar stopover may switch from a global cue to a landmark or odor.

A 2003 experiment with juvenile thrush nightingales illustrates seasonal dependence. Magnetic fields simulating a route position toward northern Egypt caused birds to accumulate more fuel in an early August trial, but not in a later trial when all birds already had larger reserves. A geomagnetic cue can therefore affect behavior only when the bird’s physiological state makes the information relevant ([Frontiers in Physiology review](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2025.1562569/full)).

Natural atmospheric odor cues are also variable. Turbulence breaks odor into intermittent filaments and packets. A shearwater movement model assumed that when odor concentration remains above a detection threshold, birds maintain near-unidirectional flight, but when it falls below threshold they change course or attempt to reacquire the cue. This makes turbulence both the carrier of information and a source of navigational uncertainty ([Scientific Reports shearwater study](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-29919-0)).

## Human-caused disturbances

### Artificial light at night

Artificial light at night can interfere with migration at three linked scales.

At the local scale, light attracts or captures birds near buildings, towers, offshore platforms, ships, and windows. Birds may slow, circle, call more often, lose a linear course, or collide with illuminated structures. At the regional scale, urban skyglow can alter flight paths and stopover distributions. At the broadest scale, it changes the night sky over hundreds of kilometers and may alter circadian timing or the visibility of celestial cues.

A systematic map screened 26,208 articles and coded 490 eligible studies involving artificial light and bird movement or distribution. The evidence was concentrated in the Northern Hemisphere, Passeriformes and Charadriiformes, and red and white wavelengths. The map identified 56 response variables across behavior, distribution, and community outcomes, but it did not find a uniform response across species or lighting conditions ([Adams et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13750-021-00246-8)).

Artificial light can potentially disrupt all three major compass systems:

- It can shift the apparent light cycle and interfere with the time-compensated sun compass.
- It can obscure, dilute, or alter the learned stellar pattern through skyglow.
- Its spectrum can affect the retinal radical-pair magnetic compass, while retinal bleaching may reduce sensitivity to dim stars or landmarks.

The proposed pathways are biologically plausible, but the size of a wild bird’s effective clock shift under outdoor lighting remains unknown. Laboratory studies show that particular wavelengths can disrupt magnetic orientation, yet many real-world lights have broad or changing spectra, and birds often retain redundant cues.

The behavioral effects of urban light are nevertheless directly demonstrated. At New York City’s annual Tribute in Light, 88 spotlights altered the flight behavior of an estimated 1.1 million migrants over seven years of radar observations. Peak densities in the beams regularly exceeded surrounding baselines by more than 20-fold and sometimes by 150-fold. Turning the lights off whenever 1,000 birds were visually detected produced a large reduction in the concentration of birds and kept mortality comparatively low ([Burt et al. review](https://lightsoutheartland.org/images/articles/Burt_TREE_2023EcolandEvolrevlighteffectsonmigration2023.pdf)).

At Chicago’s McCormick Place Convention Center, more than 40,000 dead birds were recorded through long-term spring and autumn monitoring beginning in 1978. Mortality was highest when lights were on during large migration events and winds concentrated birds along the lakeshore. The review estimated that reducing window illumination to the minimum observed level could reduce mortality by about 60%.

Artificial light can attract birds broadly while making a particular site locally unattractive. Radar studies found greater migrant density near bright skyglow at broad scales, but lower density in areas within about 1 km of high local artificial light when birds selected stopover habitat. This is not a contradiction: large-scale attraction or capture can coexist with local avoidance of illuminated stopover habitat. Cloud, fog, and mist amplify skyglow, making weather an important modifier.

The best-supported conclusion is therefore that artificial light changes movement and collision risk. Direct compass disruption is established under some controlled conditions, but the magnitude of that mechanism in free-flying migrants varies with light spectrum, intensity, direction, weather, species, and the availability of alternative cues.

### Radio-frequency electromagnetic fields

Radio-frequency electromagnetic fields must be distinguished from ordinary sound. They are electromagnetic oscillations, not acoustic noise, and their relevance follows from experiments showing that certain RF bands interfere with the radical-pair mechanism proposed for magnetic orientation.

The clearest evidence comes from European robins. In controlled hut experiments, robins could not use their magnetic compass in the electromagnetic background of unscreened wooden huts. Electrically grounded, aluminum-screened huts restored orientation while attenuating noise between 50 kilohertz and 5 megahertz by approximately two orders of magnitude. Removing the grounding or adding broadband noise again disrupted orientation ([Engels et al., 2014](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature13290)).

Additional experiments found that robins remained disoriented after exposure to 7.0 megahertz fields at 480 nanoteslas and to 1.315 megahertz fields at 15 nanoteslas, but they recovered orientation immediately after returning to the local geomagnetic field. This suggests interference while the RF field is present rather than a lasting injury. Cry1a photoreduction itself did not appear to be blocked, leaving the precise molecular point of interference unresolved ([Wiltschko et al., 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4305412/)).

Eurasian blackcaps provide important frequency-specific counterevidence. Broadband RF at 140–150 and 235–245 megahertz did not prevent birds from changing headings when the magnetic field was rotated by 120°. Earlier work had found disruption at 75–85 megahertz, placing the disruptive range somewhere above 100 kilohertz and below approximately 145 megahertz for that species and experimental design ([PNAS magnetic-compass study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10334787/)).

These experiments establish a direct causal pathway from some RF exposures to compass disruption in captive migrants. They do not yet provide a population-level exposure threshold for free-flying birds near telecommunications infrastructure. Solar activity offers a natural proxy for broadband RF noise, but large-scale banding data found inconsistent effects: fall geomagnetic disturbance was associated with vagrancy, while solar activity was not a uniform hazard and responses differed between species and between diurnal and nocturnal migrants.

### Conventional acoustic noise

Traffic, aircraft, construction, and industrial noise operate through different pathways. They can mask calls, increase vigilance, reduce feeding, alter stopover choice, or cause birds to leave suitable habitat. Direct disruption of a magnetic or celestial compass is much less firmly established.

A field playback experiment in southern Idaho broadcast traffic noise from a 0.5-km speaker array on alternating four-day noise-on and noise-off blocks during autumn migration. Noise levels were approximately 55–60 dB(A). Bird abundance along the simulated road was 28% lower during noise-on periods, while abundance at a control site rose by 3%. Thirteen of 22 individually analyzed species responded negatively, and cedar waxwings and yellow warblers almost completely avoided the array ([McClure et al., 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3826227/)).

A complementary experiment exposed white-crowned sparrows to traffic noise at about 61 dB(A). Foraging fell by approximately 8%, vigilance rose by approximately 21%, and feeding duration fell by about 30%. In the field community, 31% of birds avoided the noise and birds that remained had body condition approximately one standard deviation lower. Species differed: some stayed and paid a foraging cost, while others left and avoided the cost ([Ware et al., 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4593122/)).

These are important migration effects, but they are not direct demonstrations of compass failure. They show that conventional acoustic noise can change where birds stop, how long they remain, and how much energy they acquire. A bird that leaves a stopover early or flies on with inadequate reserves may later show poorer route performance, but that downstream pathway should not be confused with acoustic disruption of the navigation mechanism itself.

No direct field or laboratory evidence in the available studies demonstrates that ordinary traffic noise causes a migratory bird to lose its magnetic heading or geographic map. Reviews suggest that noise could mask nocturnal flight calls used by some species, but migration-specific causal tests remain limited.

### Air pollution and anthropogenic odor mixtures

Air pollution could interfere with olfactory navigation in at least three ways. It could mask natural odor gradients, add new odor mixtures that birds have not learned, or alter atmospheric chemistry so that familiar compounds are oxidized or diluted. Particulate pollution could also affect physiology, visibility, or the decision to migrate.

The direct evidence remains insufficient. The Pisa VOC study measured anthropogenic compounds including benzene, toluene, xylenes, and trimethylbenzene near a pigeon loft. These compounds formed regional gradients that could theoretically contribute to an olfactory map, but the study did not expose birds to controlled polluted mixtures or demonstrate that pollution impaired navigation.

A broader review of 225 nocturnally migrating species across the Americas, Africa–Europe, and East Asia–Australia found that artificial light and ground-level PM2.5 were positively correlated in passage regions and seasons. The strongest co-exposure occurred in the East Asia–Australia flyway. This establishes that migrants can encounter both hazards together, not that pollution causes an olfactory-map failure ([La Sorte et al., 2022](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10358689)).

A species-specific example concerns tule greater white-fronted geese (*Anser albifrons elgasi*). When PM2.5 exceeded 161 micrograms per cubic meter, the geese reportedly stopped migrating or altered direction and altitude. The evidence is consistent with extreme pollution deterring or disrupting flight, but it does not identify olfaction as the mechanism.

Thus, the strongest supported answer to the question of direct pollution effects on olfactory navigation is that no direct causal demonstration is established in the evidence considered here. The evidence supports plausible chemical interference and shows pollution-associated changes in migration behavior, but it does not identify the affected odorants, receptor thresholds, or the loss of a learned map.

### Habitat loss, landscape change, and landmark removal

Habitat loss affects migration most clearly by removing stopover sites and breaking the network of places where birds rest and refuel. This can force longer flights, alter departure and arrival timing, increase energetic costs, and reduce survival. Those effects are important but are not identical to loss of compass or map precision.

An analysis of eight waterfowl species on the East Asian–Australasian Flyway used migration networks from 1992–2015 and 2,688 count records from 24 Yangtze Basin lakes. Population change was positively related to change in functional connectivity: the coefficient was 0.24, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.04–0.44. The strongest four-year lag coefficient was 0.26. The authors interpret connectivity loss as the removal or isolation of stopover nodes, forcing longer non-stop flights or suboptimal timing ([Xu et al., 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6852588/)).

A 2025 hemispheric analysis integrated movement data from more than 329,000 birds of 112 species with projected land-cover and temperature change. It identified migratory connectivity as the strongest driver of projected risk relative to hazard and vulnerability. This is evidence for population-level exposure to landscape change, not a test of whether an individual bird loses the ability to recognize a route ([Saunders et al., 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41559-024-02575-6)).

The specific effect of removing visual landmarks is less well established. If a bird uses a coastline, river, island, mountain ridge, or urban edge to estimate lateral drift, obscuring or removing that feature could reduce correction accuracy. Yet the available evidence contains few controlled before-and-after tests in which a migratory landmark was removed while other cues were held constant. Open-ocean godwits compensate without obvious landmarks, showing that landmarks are not necessary in every context. Fog studies show that reduced visibility can alter route performance, but they do not isolate one landmark.

The evidence therefore supports a strong landscape-connectivity effect and a plausible landmark-feedback effect, while direct causal estimates of navigation-precision loss after landmark removal remain unavailable.

## Species comparisons and evidence strength

Different species reveal different parts of the navigation problem. A compass result in a nocturnal passerine should not automatically be generalized to a transoceanic shorebird, just as a pigeon homing result should not be treated as proof of a migratory map in every bird.

| Species or group | Principal finding | Navigation task | Strongest interpretation | Important limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| European robin (*Erithacus rubecula*) | Light-dependent inclination compass; delayed recalibration; RF disruption | Directional orientation | Magnetic compass is robust but plastic and vulnerable to specific RF fields | Receptor identity and free-flight exposure thresholds remain unresolved |
| Indigo bunting (*Passerina cyanea*) | Learned an artificial stellar rotation center and retained it | Star-compass development | Stellar orientation is learned during a sensitive period | Direct matched evidence for sun and polarized-light use in this species is not supplied |
| Garden warbler (*Sylvia borin*) | Inherited directional program; mixed cue-calibration results | Seasonal heading | Naïve birds can orient without a learned route; calibration is conditional | Direct migratory olfactory-map evidence is not established here |
| Eurasian reed warbler (*Acrocephalus scirpaceus*) | V1 required for 1,000-km correction; full magnetic-field displacement elicited correction | Geographic position and corridor recovery | Strongest bird evidence for geomagnetic or V1-linked position information | Sensor identity, exact coordinate computation, and generality remain uncertain |
| Lesser black-backed gull | Olfactory nerve required for unfamiliar longitudinal correction | Large-scale corridor recovery | Olfactory information can support true-navigation-like correction | Cue substitution occurs in familiar regions; no sham surgery in one study |
| Gambel’s white-crowned sparrow | Adults corrected 3,700-km displacement; juveniles followed innate direction | Continental position correction | Experience builds a large-scale map | Cue identity was not isolated |
| Common cuckoo | Young birds partially corrected 1,800-km displacement | First-migration route recovery | Juveniles may use inherited beacons or partial map information | Individual responses varied; destination was not always reached |
| Bar-tailed godwit | Nine birds crossed the Pacific in a narrow corridor and selected favorable departure winds | Oceanic route maintenance | Strong directional precision and wind selection | No cue-isolation experiment identified map versus compass |
| Hudsonian godwit | Full wind-drift compensation dominated a >7,000-km flight | Continuous route control | Birds can compensate over open ocean without obvious landmarks | Position cue and visual-feedback mechanism remain unresolved |
| Wandering albatross | Movement favored modeled high-microbarom regions during foraging | Long-range environmental movement | Infrasound may indicate distant wind and wave conditions | Foraging study, correlational, and not a migration-navigation test |

### The Pacific bar-tailed godwit: what has actually been tested?

The primary field evidence for *Limosa lapponica baueri* crossing the Pacific consists of satellite telemetry, wind analysis, and route geometry. Nine birds tracked from the south Yukon–Kuskokwim Delta in Alaska maintained an initial mean heading near 193° and followed a central-Pacific corridor less than 1,800 km wide. Seven females with implanted transmitters flew 8,117–11,680 km nonstop in 6.0–9.4 days; two males with external transmitters flew 7,008–7,390 km in 5.0–6.6 days. The tracking data were filtered using Argos location classes whose best standard fixes had an approximate 1-sigma error radius below 1,500 m, while poorer classes were removed or checked for plausibility ([Gill et al., 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2664343/)).

The study also showed that birds timed departure to favorable tailwinds. This is primary field evidence for wind selection and route maintenance. It is not a controlled test of magnetic cues, solar angles, stars, landmarks, or olfaction.

The available secondary summary says that godwits are thought to combine magnetic information, Sun angles, star movements, landmarks, and wind correction when crossing toward New Zealand. That description is ecologically plausible, but the page itself is an encyclopedia summary, not a cue-manipulation experiment ([Te Ara summary](https://teara.govt.nz/en/photograph/7253/bar-tailed-godwits-taking-off)). The Ouvéa staging record likewise documents a satellite-tracked bird encountering adverse weather and stopping in the Loyalty Islands; it does not test a navigation mechanism ([staging note](https://doi.org/10.63172/947936npouoo)).

Consequently, the strongest supported judgment is that Pacific bar-tailed godwits combine an inherited or learned directional program with wind selection and active route control. The evidence does not yet separate a compass heading from a geographic map, nor does it demonstrate direct use of landmarks or a particular magnetic coordinate.

### What does conventional acoustic-noise research show?

The field and laboratory evidence shows that conventional acoustic noise can alter stopover distribution, vigilance, foraging, body condition, and the decision to remain in a habitat. The Idaho traffic-playback experiment used 55–60 dB(A) noise and found a 28% reduction in bird abundance along the phantom road, with 13 of 22 species responding negatively. The white-crowned-sparrow laboratory experiment used 61 dB(A) and found reduced foraging and feeding duration and increased vigilance.

These outcomes matter for migration because a bird that avoids or abandons a stopover may lose energy needed for later route correction. However, none of these studies directly measured magnetic headings, celestial orientation, map correction, or successful completion of migration. The direct evidence for conventional noise disrupting a compass or map is therefore unavailable in the studies considered here.

### What direct evidence exists for air pollution or anthropogenic odor mixtures?

Direct causal evidence is not established in the available literature. The strongest partial evidence consists of three different observations:

1. Near Pisa, anthropogenic aromatic compounds formed measurable regional gradients alongside natural DMS and terpenes. This shows that pollution-related compounds could be part of an odor environment, not that birds use or are confused by them.

2. Across 225 nocturnally migrating species in three flyways, artificial light and PM2.5 were positively correlated in seasonal passage regions. This documents co-exposure rather than navigational impairment.

3. Tule greater white-fronted geese reportedly stopped or altered direction and altitude when PM2.5 exceeded 161 micrograms per cubic meter. This is a migration response to severe pollution, but the sensory pathway is unknown.

No supplied study directly compared olfactory navigation under clean air with navigation under an anthropogenic odor mixture while measuring route correction in a migratory species. The affected odorants, receptor thresholds, and whether pollution masks or replaces learned odors remain unavailable.

### What direct evidence exists for habitat and landmark removal?

Direct tests of navigation precision after removing or obscuring a migratory landmark are also not established in the available evidence. The strongest results concern landscape connectivity: habitat loss removes stopover nodes, reduces refueling opportunities, and may force longer or riskier flights. The eight-waterfowl analysis and the hemispheric 112-species risk study support those population and route-network effects.

The visual-landmark mechanism is supported indirectly. Fog changes route direction and drift compensation, and theoretical models propose that angular landmark movement helps birds estimate lateral displacement. Yet no supplied experiment removes a known coastline, river, mountain, island, or urban feature and measures the resulting change in route accuracy while controlling magnetic, celestial, wind, and olfactory cues.

Thus, habitat change can clearly impair migration feasibility without impairing the sensory compass itself. Landmark loss may additionally reduce local position correction, but its magnitude is not quantified.

### What has been quantified about precision, error correction, and cue substitution?

The available evidence is quantitative but fragmented rather than comparable as one global statistic.

For experienced adults, the strongest displacement results include:

- Reed warblers correcting a 1,000-km eastward displacement when V1 was intact, but not after V1 sectioning.
- White-crowned sparrow adults correcting a 3,700-km transcontinental displacement while juveniles followed their innate direction.
- Lesser black-backed gulls correcting a 1,080-km unfamiliar westward displacement when olfaction was intact, but not after olfactory-nerve section.
- Adult Hudsonian godwits showing full compensation in 41.1% of classified segments and approximately 39.4% total drift during a >7,000-km transoceanic flight.

For juveniles and first-time migrants:

- Juvenile blackcaps, garden warblers, and willow warblers shifted headings after an 1,100-km displacement, but the target of correction was ambiguous.
- Young common cuckoos partially corrected an 1,800-km displacement, with variable endpoints.
- Juvenile white-crowned sparrows did not correct a 3,700-km displacement in free flight.
- First-year birds may use inherited programs plus beacons rather than a complete map.

For nocturnal versus diurnal migrants, the evidence is uneven. Nocturnal passerines have the richest controlled compass literature because their orientation can be tested in Emlen funnels. Diurnal and soaring migrants are better represented by radar and telemetry. The 93-bird telemetry analysis found greater route deviation at night, but species, weather, wind, and magnetic inclination also mattered. Bar-tailed godwits showed low deviation in that comparison, whereas tundra swans showed higher deviation.

No study supplied here quantifies a universal switching rule such as “birds switch from magnetic to olfactory cues after a particular distance” or “juveniles achieve a specified angular error.” The evidence supports conditional substitution, not a common numerical algorithm.

### What evidence exists for auditory or infrasonic migration cues?

The migration-specific evidence remains absent or preliminary. The most relevant primary study tracked 89 wandering albatrosses during foraging trips and found movement toward modeled microbarom sound pressure. It did not manipulate infrasound, measure albatross hearing thresholds, or test migration direction.

The physical case for infrasound is strong: microbaroms travel thousands of kilometers and are associated with ocean waves and storms. The biological case is weaker. Infrasonic hearing has been directly confirmed in only a small number of bird species, and no supplied study demonstrates that a migrating bird uses anthropogenic infrasound to select or correct a route.

Conventional auditory cues, such as nocturnal flight calls, may also influence group movement or orientation, but the available review evidence presents this as a possibility rather than a demonstrated global mechanism. Infrasound and ordinary acoustic noise should therefore not be merged: the former is a candidate long-range environmental cue, while the latter is a demonstrated disturbance of habitat use and behavior but not yet of the compass or map.

## Established mechanisms, contested explanations, and evidence limits

Several conclusions are now robust.

First, birds possess multiple directional compasses. Magnetic inclination orientation, time-compensated solar orientation, polarized skylight, and learned stellar orientation are supported by repeated behavioral experiments across several species.

Second, birds can combine heading information with geographic position information. Large displacement corrections in reed warblers, white-crowned sparrows, gulls, cuckoos, and some juvenile passerines cannot be explained by an unmodified inherited direction alone.

Third, cue integration is flexible. Experience, age, season, horizon visibility, migration stage, weather, route familiarity, and energetic condition all change which cue appears dominant.

Fourth, wind correction is not a minor adjustment. It is a central component of route maintenance, including during long oceanic flights. Bar-tailed and Hudsonian godwits show that birds can preserve a narrow route or compensate for crosswind even where visual landmarks are scarce.

Other explanations remain contested.

The radical-pair account is the leading explanation for the light-dependent magnetic compass, but the in-vivo receptor and downstream neural conversion are not settled. Magnetite, trigeminal, and inner-ear hypotheses remain part of the debate, particularly for map-like magnetic information.

A universal geomagnetic bi-coordinate map is not established. Reed warblers respond to realistic combinations of magnetic parameters, but responses to declination alone are inconsistent across studies and species. The Earth’s field does not form a regular global grid, and repeated magnetic signatures can produce ambiguity.

An olfactory map is strongly supported in homing pigeons and in some displaced gull and seabird experiments, but its form is disputed. Birds might compare odor mixtures with learned wind directions, follow corridor-derived plumes, or use olfaction only when other information is weak. The relevant molecules, receptor thresholds, and persistence of mixtures remain unknown.

Visual landmarks are clearly useful at some scales, but direct tests of long-distance landmark use are limited. The ability of godwits to compensate over open ocean demonstrates that landmarks are not necessary for every correction, not that they are unimportant near coasts or destinations.

Infrasound is physically plausible and supported by a correlational albatross movement study, but migration-navigation causality has not been demonstrated. Anthropogenic infrasound has not been shown to disrupt a migratory compass.

Human disturbances also differ in evidentiary strength. Artificial light reliably alters nocturnal movement, aggregation, collision risk, and distribution. RF electromagnetic fields can directly disrupt magnetic orientation under controlled conditions. Conventional noise reliably changes stopover behavior and energetic state, but direct compass effects are unproven. Air pollution, habitat loss, and landmark change have strong or plausible ecological pathways, but direct losses of migratory map precision have not been quantified.

## Closing judgment

Migratory birds navigate precisely because they operate a redundant, adaptive system rather than a single sensory instrument. Magnetic, solar, stellar, polarized-light, olfactory, visual, atmospheric, and wind information can each contribute different kinds of information at different spatial scales. Experience allows birds to learn maps, beacons, corridors, and calibration relationships, while wind-drift compensation continuously corrects the flight path.

The most secure scientific distinction is between a compass that maintains direction and a map-like process that estimates position. Compass mechanisms are comparatively well established; the map is multifactorial, species-dependent, and still unresolved. Disturbances are most damaging when they remove several cues at once—for example, strong crosswinds under heavy cloud, or artificial light combined with urban structures and poor visibility. Birds’ navigational resilience ultimately depends less on any single “best” cue than on their ability to compare, recalibrate, and substitute among imperfect sources of information.
